personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Draco is defined by a consistent pattern of sneering arrogance, class-conscious contempt, performative cruelty, and cowardice beneath a bully's bluster. His voice is drawling and superior; he talks loudly so others hear him, uses 'Mudblood' without flinching, taunts from positions of safety (with Crabbe and Goyle flanking him, or under Snape's protection), and retreats when his position weakens. He is also genuinely petulant and dependent on his father—bragging about Lucius constantly, using paternal influence as both weapon and shield. He shows fear in the Forest (shaking, admitting he is scared), escalating in HBP into a boy visibly cracking under impossible pressure: grey-faced, losing weight, crying in the bathroom. His sneering confidence is a performance that collapses when real danger arrives. He has observable contradictions: he is cruel to the powerless but flinches before the powerful; he pursues status but is never truly independent of his father; he claims to want to be chosen but is terrified of what that means.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films capture the surface pattern well: the drawling contempt, the crowd-playing insults ('That's right, Weasley… my father can afford the best'), the sneering at Hagrid's class, calling Hermione a Mudblood, wielding prefect/Inquisitorial Squad authority petulantly. Tom Felton consistently uses shorter, clipped delivery with a sneer and an upward tilt of contempt that matches the book's 'bored, drawling voice.' The cowardice in the Forest is preserved (the scream, fleeing Buckbeak's attack with a theatrical wound, the arm-in-sling faking). In HBP, the films preserve the grey, hollow look, the crying bathroom scene, and the rooftop confrontation where his hand trembles and he admits 'I've got to kill you or he'll kill me.' The key traits—performative dominance, paternal dependence, fragility under pressure—are present.
personality_voice.difference: The films lose some of the sustained verbal texture. Book Draco has extended monologues in the Slytherin common room (Polyjuice scene), sustained cruelty campaigns over weeks (the 'Potter Stinks' badge, the Quidditch commentary, the dementor impressions), and sharp throwaway lines that reveal his worldview constantly. The films compress and streamline. Several set-pieces of his verbal cruelty are cut entirely (the hospital wing taunting of Ron, the Hogsmeade insults before Hermione punches him, the repeated mockery of Hagrid's class over the term). The film Draco is recognizably the same character but with less sustained register of his constant low-level psychological warfare. His voice is intact but its frequency is reduced.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main traits, flaws, tone, and contradictions are preserved, earning a score in the 18–22 range. The compression of his sustained verbal cruelty and several key speech patterns—particularly his extended gloating and scheming in private settings—constitutes minor simplification of secondary traits. The HBP shift in personality is preserved well in the films. No major trait is reversed or invented.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Draco serves several simultaneous narrative functions across the series: primary school antagonist and foil to Harry, embodiment of pure-blood supremacist ideology made personal and immediate, agent of threat and sabotage (the Remembrall, the Hippogriff complaint, the Polyjuice trap, the diary plot, the Buckbeak execution campaign, the necklace/poisoned mead/Vanishing Cabinet missions in HBP), and ultimately a moral test case—the character through whom Rowling asks whether a child shaped by evil can choose differently. In the Deathly Hallows, he functions as the inadvertent master of the Elder Wand (structural pivot of the entire final arc) and as a reluctant identifier at Malfoy Manor whose non-identification effectively saves Harry. His agency is high: he initiates confrontations, schemes independently, manipulates events, and his choices affect outcomes. In HBP, he is the primary antagonist driving the plot's central threat.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Draco's antagonist function through Philosophers Stone, Chamber, Prisoner, and Goblet reasonably well. His role as Hagrid's accuser in PoA, his campaign against Buckbeak, and his initiating the Polyjuice interrogation scene are intact. In HBP, his function as the central threat is preserved: the Vanishing Cabinet plot, the Astronomy Tower confrontation, his recruitment into Death Eater service are all present. The Elder Wand pivot (that Draco disarmed Dumbledore and Harry later disarmed Draco, making Harry the wand's master) is preserved and explicitly stated in DH2. His refusal to identify Harry at Malfoy Manor is retained in the film. The Inquisitorial Squad role in OotP is present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several specific acts of agency are reduced or cut. In PoA, the book Draco actively organizes the Death Eater prank at the Quidditch match to frighten Harry with fake dementors; in the film he is simply part of a group, with less individual cunning shown. His extended scheme to get Hagrid fired through the Buckbeak case—including visiting him in the hospital wing to taunt Ron, coaching his father's Ministry involvement—is compressed. The book's OotP Draco as Inquisitorial Squad member actively using power over students (docking points, cornering Harry) is shown in the film but with less sustained agency. Most significantly, the book's HBP Draco independently devises the entire Vanishing Cabinet plan, rejects Snape's help, uses Polyjuice to disguise Crabbe and Goyle as lookouts, and coordinates the entire Death Eater entry—all of this is his own scheming. The film shows the result (the cabinet working, Death Eaters arriving) but telescopes his independent strategic thinking. The scene where Draco refuses Snape's help and insists 'this is my moment' is present in both but the film gives less evidence of his actual operational choices.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Role and agency are clearly present and mostly preserved. Some reduction in specific acts of individual cunning and initiative—particularly the book's extended PoA antagonist scheming and the HBP operational details—constitutes a moderate reduction. The key structural functions (Elder Wand pivot, Manor identification refusal, HBP central threat) are intact. Score in the 14–17 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Draco's motivations in the early books are relatively simple: social dominance, pure-blood supremacy internalized from Lucius, and rivalry with Harry. These are legible in his every action. The deeper motivational structure emerges in HBP: he is given a mission he cannot refuse without his family being killed; he genuinely wants to prove himself to Voldemort and escape his father's shadow (his own pride and ambition); he simultaneously fears death and recognizes that killing is beyond him; he is afraid of Voldemort more than he is loyal to him. His internal conflict at the Astronomy Tower—wand shaking, lowering it before the Death Eaters arrive—is the book's clearest evidence that his motivations are layered: he wants the glory but not the act, he wants survival but not at any cost, he is torn between the ideology he was raised in and a self-preservation instinct that carries faint moral content. In DH, his motivation at Malfoy Manor is pure self-preservation and family loyalty, with the refusal to confirm Harry's identity suggesting some residual decency or simply cowardice about the consequences of being wrong.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core motivational shift from HBP onward reasonably well. The Astronomy Tower scene includes his admission 'I've got to kill you or he'll kill me,' making the coercion explicit. The film preserves the tension between his pride ('I was chosen!') and his fear. His unwillingness to kill Dumbledore, the lowering of the wand, the reliance on Death Eaters arriving to save him from having to act—all present. In DH, his ambiguous non-identification at Malfoy Manor is preserved. His father's cowardice and the family's collective degradation under Voldemort is shown clearly in both the Deathly Hallows scenes and the opening Malfoy Manor table sequence.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films lose the nuance of Draco's specific internal justifications and the ideological dimension of his conflict. In the books, he genuinely believes in blood purity early on—it's not just something he's been told, it shapes his contempt authentically. The films show the behavior but slightly flatten the ideology into pure social snobbery. Also lost: in HBP, book Draco's strategic thinking and active scheming (trying to fix the cabinet, recruiting help, testing objects) is presented as driven partly by his desire for independent glory—to eclipse Lucius. The film compresses this into a more generically frightened boy carrying out a mission. The 'I wanted this, I chose this' dimension of his pride is present but underweighted.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations are simplified but not reversed. The coercion, the family loyalty, the fear, and the clash between pride and terror are present. The loss of the deeper ideological conviction and the specific texture of his desire for independent glory from under Lucius's shadow constitutes simplification without falsification. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Draco's arc across the series is a descent followed by an ambiguous non-resolution. Starting point: arrogant, confident, buoyed by paternal prestige and pure-blood ideology. Key turning point: CoS, where he gloats over Dumbledore's suspension and reveals his dependence on Lucius's power rather than any independent strength. PoA: first cracks appear—the Hippogriff incident exposes how his arrogance triggers real consequences, and he milks the injury in a way that reveals his understanding of power as performance. GoF: his cruelty escalates but his father's public humiliation at the World Cup and his own relative diminishment (not in the Tournament, outperformed by Harry repeatedly) begins to corrode his confidence. OotP: Draco reaches his highest institutional power (Inquisitorial Squad, prefect) but it is entirely derivative of Umbridge and Fudge, not his own. HBP: The arc's climax—Draco is broken down entirely. He is physically grey and gaunt, crying in bathrooms, rejecting all help out of desperate pride, nearly killing innocent people through incompetent proxy attacks, and finally unable to kill Dumbledore. The arc does not resolve into redemption. DH: He is the passive son in a degraded family, making one ambiguous choice (not confirming Harry's identity) that may be cowardice or conscience, and at the Battle of Hogwarts he is saved by Harry—a man he has spent years persecuting—then goes to his parents. The epilogue shows him older, nodding curtly to Harry, still separate. It is an arc of hubris-to-collapse without full redemption.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films trace the broad shape of this arc adequately. His confident early cruelty, the escalating antagonism, the HBP breakdown (grey face, bathroom scene, Astronomy Tower confrontation where his hand shakes), the passive DH role, and the final ambiguous curtly-nodded epilogue are all present. The Room of Requirement sequence in DH2 adds a small active moment (he goes to Hogwarts, calls Blaise and Goyle, confronts Harry, then is saved by Harry) that preserves some version of his DH arc.
character_arc.difference: The arc's intermediate steps—particularly from GoF through OotP—are significantly compressed. In the books, the gradual erosion of Draco's standing and confidence across these years is built through dozens of scenes and small defeats. The film reduces his GoF presence substantially (he appears mainly for insults and the ferret scene) and his OotP institutional power (the Inquisitorial Squad) is shown but not developed into the extended arc of petty tyranny followed by humiliation that the book builds. The key book moment in HBP where Draco's increasing desperation is tracked over months—the failed assassination attempts, the worsening physical condition, the rejected Snape overtures—is compressed into fewer, cleaner scenes. The arc exists but several important steps are skipped or rushed. The epilogue beat is present but brief.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but recognizable. Key turning points (HBP breakdown, Astronomy Tower crisis, DH ambiguity, epilogue) are present. The loss of the gradual year-by-year erosion and several specific arc-steps (GoF positioning, OotP institutional rise and fall) constitutes an incomplete arc that misses important steps. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Draco's most defining relationships: (1) Lucius—a relationship of imitation, dependence, and eventually terrifying inheritance; Draco becomes Lucius, then surpasses him in risk, and ultimately finds himself in a situation Lucius created for him. The power dynamic shifts in HBP from admiration to a mission that is partly punishment for Lucius's failure. (2) Harry—pure antagonism that reveals both characters; Draco's hatred of Harry is partly about Harry refusing to need or want what Draco offers (the handshake, the offer of friendship in book 1). (3) Snape—a relationship of real affection and trust on Draco's side early on (Snape is 'Draco's favourite teacher') that turns to resentment and suspicion in HBP when Draco sees Snape's offer of help as competition for glory rather than genuine protection. (4) Narcissa—deep maternal bond that shapes his choices in DH; her question 'Is Draco alive?' is the hinge of Harry's survival.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Harry-Draco antagonism is well preserved across all films. The Lucius-Draco relationship is present—the purchasing of brooms, the bookshop confrontation, the Malfoy Manor degradation in DH. Narcissa's protection of Draco (including the Unbreakable Vow scene and the lying-to-Voldemort moment in DH2) is preserved. The Snape-Draco relationship in HBP is present in the corridor scene ('I was chosen! This is my moment!') and the Astronomy Tower.
key_relationships.difference: The Snape-Draco relationship loses most of its texture. In the books, Draco's genuine fondness for Snape (calling him his favourite teacher, currying favour) and the specific betrayal he feels when Snape seems to be trying to steal his mission is clearly developed. The film gives us the confrontation result but not the prior warmth that makes Draco's resentment legible. The Lucius-Draco relationship loses the specific dynamic of Draco idolizing and then being abandoned by Lucius—the book tracks this over multiple years, culminating in Lucius being entirely ineffectual in DH while Draco navigates alone. This is present but compressed in the films. The Narcissa-Draco relationship is probably the best-preserved of the four, particularly in DH2.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Most key relationships are present but some are simplified. The Snape-Draco relationship in particular loses the warmth-to-resentment arc that makes Draco's HBP isolation more tragic. The Lucius-Draco dynamic is present but the specific escalation from idealized paternal figure to liability is compressed. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Draco's richness in the books comes from several sources: (1) sustained verbal cruelty as a consistent behavioral register—not just single insults but ongoing campaigns of psychological warfare; (2) his cowardice being specific and legible—he retreats, fakes, maneuvers; it is not just general timidity but strategic avoidance of personal risk; (3) his ideological conviction being genuine, not merely performed—he really believes blood purity matters, which makes his eventual inability to act on it (killing Dumbledore) more interesting; (4) the contradiction between his stated values and his actual behavior—he claims pure-blood superiority but is repeatedly outperformed by Hermione, whom he despises; (5) the gradual revelation that everything about him is derivative: his power, his position, his views, even his school friendships (Crabbe and Goyle are followers, not friends); (6) the bathroom scene in HBP as a genuinely shocking revelation—this character who has functioned as cruel antagonist for five books is revealed to be a frightened, crying teenager; (7) moments of near-decency that are never fully resolved—the rooftop lowering of the wand, the Manor non-identification.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films capture several of these: the cowardice is visible (the ferret, the screaming at Buckbeak, the bathroom tears, the trembling hand on the tower). The ideological contempt is present in the Mudblood slur and the Slytherin common room scene. The bathroom breakdown is in the film. The rooftop confrontation preserves the moral ambiguity. The Manor non-identification is retained. Tom Felton's performance adds physical specificity that the text cannot—the grey skin, the haunted eyes.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: What the films lose: (1) The sustained verbal campaign texture—in the books, Draco's cruelty is a constant background hum across every year; the films reduce it to set-pieces. (2) The book's careful tracking of his ideological conviction—we see him act on it (the 'Mudbloods' comment, the Inquisitorial Squad), but the films don't develop the depth of his belief or the irony of Hermione consistently beating him. (3) The Polyjuice scene in CoS, where Draco unknowingly reveals to Harry that he doesn't know who the Heir is ('I wish I knew'), is preserved but its comic-tragic irony (the great schemer doesn't know) is flattened. (4) Several scenes that deepen his complexity are cut: the Hogsmeade mud-throwing scene from PoA (showing Harry's satisfaction at anonymous retaliation), the extended hospital wing taunting in HBP, the multiple failed Slughorn approaches. (5) Crabbe and Goyle's explicit breaking from Draco's authority in DH2 ('You and your dad are finished') is actually present in the film corpus and adds useful texture. (6) The book's explicit statement that Draco was moved by Dumbledore's offer—that he was 'lowering his wand'—is preserved in the film, but the build-up over multiple chapters showing his growing desperation makes the rooftop moment more earned in the books.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification has occurred. Several important nuances are missing or reduced—particularly the sustained ideological texture, the comedy of his ignorance in CoS, the extended HBP desperation arc, and the precise mechanics of how his cowardice functions as strategic avoidance rather than simple fear. The character remains substantially legible but the material that makes him rich is thinner in the films. Score in the 8–10 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Extended verbal cruelty campaigns across each school year (the sustained psychological warfare in books is compressed to isolated set-pieces in films)
Draco's active hospital wing taunting of Ron during the dragon subplot in PS/SS
The full Hogsmeade mud-throwing sequence (PoA) including Harry's invisible retaliation and Draco's subsequent report to Snape
Draco's systematic fake-dementor stunt at the Quidditch match in PoA (in the book, an active scheme; in the film, reduced presence)
The extended Quidditch match commentary insults in PoA, particularly the 'Weasley is our King' campaign coordinated by Draco
Draco's months-long operational management of the HBP Vanishing Cabinet plan—including the Polyjuice lookout system using Crabbe and Goyle as girls, which is referenced in the film but not developed
The Slytherin common room scene's full irony: Draco not knowing who the Heir is undercuts his pretensions to insider knowledge (present in film but less developed)
Draco's gradual ideological conviction being shown as genuine rather than performative—the books build evidence of real belief in blood purity, not just social snobbery
The specific Snape-Draco warmth established over five books (Draco calling Snape his favourite teacher, the preferential Potions treatment) that makes HBP's resentment more legible
Lucius's progressive diminishment from feared patriarch to liability across GoF-OotP-HBP-DH, which contextualizes Draco's mission as partly a consequence of his father's failures

Several scenes tracking Draco's physical deterioration in HBP (grey skin, haggard appearance) beyond the key bathroom scene—the sustained physical decline is present in the film but less systematically built
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (above 75) considered but not triggered: no single core book function, decision, or emotional beat is cleanly transferred to another character. The Elder Wand pivot, the Manor non-identification, and the Astronomy Tower confrontation all remain Draco's.
Cap 1 (above 85) not applicable given the noticeable simplification of complexity and nuance across multiple dimensions.
comparative.key_observations: Draco Malfoy is one of the more faithfully adapted secondary characters in the HP films, with Tom Felton's performance preserving the essential personality, voice, and arc. The films successfully maintain the core character: the sneering arrogance, the cowardice beneath it, the HBP breakdown, the ambiguous moral moments (rooftop, Malfoy Manor). What is lost is primarily texture and depth rather than substance—the sustained verbal campaign across years, the ideological genuineness of his blood-purity beliefs, the specific mechanics of his operational scheming in HBP, and the warmth-to-resentment arc with Snape. The character is recognizably faithful but the films present a somewhat leaner version, retaining the dramatic peaks while compressing the sustained behavioural patterns that make those peaks earned. The total score of 72 reflects a faithful but noticeably simplified adaptation that loses the material richness rather than misrepresenting the core character.
